Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: This, Allies, God

outputs.L1:
“This synod is convinced that the forces of the Allies are being used of God to vindicate the rights of the weak and to maintain the moral order of the world.”  
—Anglican Synod, Melbourne, 1916

Bit weird at first:  
that starey look in the eyes,  
the hair down past his shoulders.  
But after a go with the ship’s barber,  
a sea-water shower, and the old slouch hat  
across his ears,  
he started to look the part.

Took him a while to get the way  
a bayonet fits the old Lee-Enfield,  
but going in on the boats,  
he looked calmer than any of us,  
just gazing in over the swell,  
where the cliffs looked black against the sky.

When we hit, he fairly raced in through the waves,  
then up the beach,  
swerving like a full-back at the end,  
when the Turks had really got on to us.  
By the time we all caught up,  
he was off like a flash, up the cliffs,  
after his first machine gun.

He’d done for three Turks when we got there;  
the fourth was a gibbering mess.  
Seeing him wave that blood-red bayonet,  
I reckoned we were glad  
to have him on the side.
outputs.L2:
The synod holds the firm belief that God is employing the Allied armies to defend the claims of the powerless and to uphold the world’s ethical order.  
— Anglican Synod, Melbourne, 1916

At the beginning, he seemed a little strange:  
that fixed, staring expression in his eyes,  
his hair hanging below his shoulders.  

But once the ship’s barber had dealt with him,  
after a wash in seawater,  
and with the old slouch hat pulled down  
over his ears,  
he began to appear like a soldier.

It took some time before he understood  
how the bayonet locked onto  
the old Lee-Enfield rifle.  

Yet as we approached in the boats,  
he seemed steadier than the rest of us,  
looking quietly across the rolling water  
towards the cliffs,  
dark against the sky.

When we landed,  
he rushed hard through the surf,  
then drove up the beach,  
dodging from side to side like a full-back near the line,  
just as the Turks had properly found our range.

By the time the rest of us reached him,  
he had already shot ahead,  
scrambling up the cliffs  
towards his first machine gun.

When we arrived,  
three Turks were already dead by his hand,  
and the fourth was reduced to babbling terror.

Watching him brandish that bayonet,  
red with blood,  
I thought we were fortunate  
that he was fighting for our side.
outputs.L3:
In 1916, the Anglican Synod in Melbourne presented the Allied war effort as both morally justified and divinely supported. The conflict was not described simply as a political or military struggle, but as a righteous cause in which God’s favour rested with the Allies. This religious framing helped to give the war a sense of sacred purpose, suggesting that participation in the fighting could be understood as a duty aligned with Christian values and divine will.

The poem reflects this wartime mindset through its depiction of an unusual recruit. At first, the recruit appears strange and out of place, seemingly unsuited to the discipline and appearance expected of a soldier. However, once he is subjected to military grooming, dressed in uniform, and equipped for combat, he is transformed into a recognisable fighting man. This transformation suggests that the army has the power to reshape even the most unlikely individual into a useful instrument of war.

During the landing, the recruit shows remarkable composure. While the troops come under Turkish fire, he does not panic or hesitate. Instead, he remains calm and charges fearlessly onto the beach. His courage marks him as an effective soldier, even if his behaviour and character still seem unusual to those around him.

In battle, the recruit proves to be not only brave but brutally efficient. He kills several Turkish soldiers and inspires terror in another, demonstrating a savage effectiveness that makes him valuable in combat. The poem does not soften the violence; instead, it presents the recruit’s capacity for killing as central to his usefulness.

By the end, the speaker concludes that the recruit’s strangeness and violence matter less than the fact that he is fighting for the speaker’s side. Although he may be unsettling, he is accepted because his aggression is directed against the enemy. The poem therefore exposes a wartime logic in which brutality can be excused, or even praised, when it serves the interests of one’s own nation and cause.
outputs.L4:
The text offers a sharp critique of wartime religious nationalism by setting two very different kinds of writing against one another. On one side is a 1916 Anglican endorsement of the Allied cause, a statement that presents the war as morally justified and implicitly aligns Christian faith with national and imperial duty. On the other side is a satirical battlefield narrative in which a Christ-like figure is imagined being reshaped into an ANZAC soldier. By placing these visions side by side, the text reveals how religious language can be used to bless violence and transform war into something apparently sacred.

The Anglican endorsement reflects a familiar wartime tendency: the attempt to frame military conflict as a righteous struggle between good and evil. In this view, the Allies are not merely political or military participants; they become instruments of divine justice. Such rhetoric gives war a spiritual purpose and reassures believers that fighting, killing, and sacrifice are compatible with Christian values. Religion is made to serve the nation, and the nation’s cause is made to appear holy.

The satirical battlefield narrative undermines this confidence. By imagining a Christ-like figure being converted into an ANZAC soldier, it exposes the grotesque contradiction between the teachings associated with Christ—mercy, peace, humility, and forgiveness—and the brutal demands of modern warfare. The image is disturbing because it suggests that Christ himself must be altered before he can be made useful to the war effort. His compassion has to be replaced by aggression; his suffering has to be redirected into patriotic violence. The satire therefore shows that wartime culture does not truly follow Christ so much as remake him in its own militarised image.

The key effect of this juxtaposition is to expose the moral absurdity of sanctifying violence. When religious faith is absorbed into nationalism, it can be distorted until brutality appears righteous and even necessary. Killing can be described as service, obedience to the state can be confused with obedience to God, and the horrors of the battlefield can be hidden beneath noble language about sacrifice and duty. The text challenges this transformation by showing how unnatural and ethically troubling it is.

Ultimately, the work suggests that the fusion of Christianity and wartime nationalism corrupts both religion and moral judgment. Instead of questioning violence, faith is used to legitimise it. Instead of offering an alternative to hatred and destruction, religious language becomes part of the machinery that sustains them. Through satire and contrast, the text forces readers to confront the contradiction between the message of Christ and the violence carried out in his name. Its central criticism is that once war is made sacred, people become able to excuse almost anything.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem imagining Jesus joining the ANZAC landing at Gallipoli, preceded by a 1916 Anglican Synod quotation about the Allies doing God’s work.
counterfactuals.output:
> “We are doing God’s work in this war.”  
> — attributed to an Anglican Synod, 1916

He came in no general’s coat,  
no Sam Browne belt,  
no polished boots catching the dawn.

He came barefoot,  
salt-white with spray,  
standing where the oars knocked  
against the dark hulls,  
where boys from Ballarat, Otago,  
Sydney, Christchurch, Fremantle  
held their breath  
and checked their rifles  
as if touch could make fear obedient.

No one noticed at first.

There were too many things to notice:  
the black cliffs shouldering the morning,  
the wrong beach,  
the shingle grinding under keels,  
the sudden stitching of machine guns  
from the scrub above,  
the sea lifting and lowering the boats  
like a chest that could not stop grieving.

He stepped into the water  
with the first of them.

Not ahead,  
not behind—  
among.

The tide reddened around his ankles.

A private cursed and fell.  
Jesus knelt beside him,  
pressed both hands to the wound  
as if the body were bread  
breaking again and again  
in his palms.

“Padre?” someone gasped.

But he had no cross on his collar,  
only the old one in his eyes.

All morning he climbed with them  
through thorn and dust,  
past packs split open,  
past letters from mothers,  
past biscuits, bayonets,  
the stunned mouths of the dead  
filling with flies and light.

At Plugge’s Plateau  
he carried water.

At Shrapnel Gully  
he tore his robe for bandages.

At Quinn’s Post  
he listened to a boy whisper  
that he was sorry—  
not for dying,  
but for being afraid.

Jesus said nothing grand.

He did not bless the guns.

He did not steady the officer’s hand  
over the map.

He did not say  
Empire,  
or destiny,  
or righteous cause.

He only held the boy  
until the boy’s fear went out  
like a candle cupped from wind.

By noon his hands were everywhere:  
under a Turk’s head,  
beneath an Australian’s shoulders,  
closing the eyes of a man  
who had shouted for his mother  
in a language no one near him knew.

When the chaplains prayed for victory,  
he was down among the stretcher-bearers.

When the admirals watched from offshore,  
he was sinking to his knees in the scrub.

When men cried,  
“God is with us,”  
he looked across the ridge  
to where other men,  
also beloved,  
also terrified,  
also certain God was near,  
loaded and fired  
and fell.

By evening the hills had become  
a terrible altar.

The gulls turned above it.  
The smoke drifted.  
The sea kept arriving,  
blue and indifferent,  
washing the stones  
as if forgiveness were a tide  
too late for the living  
but faithful to the dead.

And Jesus,  
bloodied to the elbows,  
sat among the wounded  
with no answer  
that could fit inside a sermon.

Only this:

not in the charge,  
not in the shellburst,  
not in the flags lifted over graves,  
not in the mouths of men  
who send other men to die—

but here,  
where one enemy gives another water,  
where a hand refuses to let go,  
where the last word spoken  
is a name loved at home,

there,  
he said,  
if anywhere,

God’s work begins.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a darkly ironic Australian war poem in colloquial voice about Christ being turned into a soldier at Gallipoli, ending with the speaker glad he is “on our side.”
counterfactuals.output:
They marched Him up from Anzac Cove,  
bare feet in the bloody clay,  
and some bloke found a slouch hat  
and tipped His halo away.  

“Can’t have that shine, mate — draws the Turks,”  
the sergeant says, real dry.  
So Christ just nods and shoulders on,  
with shrapnel in the sky.  

They gave Him bully beef for tea,  
a rifle, boots, and pack,  
and taught Him how to bayonet  
a shadow stumbling back.  

He’d healed the sick in Galilee,  
so stretcher-bearers cheered:  
“Good on ya, Jesus, you’ll be handy  
when the next lot’s disappeared.”  

But orders came at half-past four  
to take a ridge of stone;  
He asked if mercy counted much.  
They said, “Not here, my own.”  

So up He went with all the boys,  
through scrub and smoke and cries,  
the Man of Sorrows, khaki-clad,  
with dust stuck in His eyes.  

And when He fell, they dragged Him clear  
then shoved Him back once more —  
“Three days? You beauty. That’s the stuff  
we’re lookin’ for in war.”  

Now chaplains preach Him soft and mild,  
with lambs and peaceful light,  
but I seen Christ at Gallipoli,  
taught proper how to fight.  

And though it’s queer, and black as hell,  
I’ll say it, since He died:  
with Him enlisted in our mob,  
I’m glad He’s on our side.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poem that satirizes wartime Christianity and imperial propaganda by placing a long-haired holy figure among Australian troops during the Gallipoli campaign.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Man in the Slouch Hat**

They landed him at dawn one day,  
Barefoot on the shingle,  
With hair like ropes of sunburnt wheat  
And eyes no bugle could jingle.  
The chaplain said, “Good Lord, that beard—  
He’ll frighten half the nation,”  
But the sergeant spat and muttered, “Mate,  
He’ll do for ammunition.”

He walked beside the stretcher-bearers,  
Up the scrubby rise,  
Where empires carved their sermons out  
In telegrams and lies.  
The gulls cried “Glory!” overhead,  
The guns said “King and Duty,”  
And shrapnel wrote its iron psalms  
On innocence and beauty.

They gave him tea in a bully tin,  
A biscuit hard as doctrine;  
He blessed the flies, the lice, the dead,  
And every sun-cracked water-skin.  
“Which side are you?” the colonel barked,  
His moustache stiff with thunder.  
The stranger looked at Suvla’s smoke  
And softly answered, “Under.”

“Under?” cried the polished brass,  
“By God, man, speak more plainly!  
Are you with Christendom and Crown,  
Or with the Turk ungainly?”  
He touched the mud on a private’s sleeve,  
The blood on a young man’s laces:  
“I am with all the boys whose names  
Are missing from your phrases.”

The padre preached on sacrifice,  
On heaven’s bright battalion,  
While generals drew red arrows through  
A map worth more than talons.  
“Bless our arms,” the prayer began,  
“Confound the foe’s resistance—”  
The long-haired man blew out the lamp  
And blessed the whole existence.

He healed no wound with trumpet-call,  
No sermon stopped the bleeding;  
He only held the frightened hands  
Of lads the Empire was needing.  
A drover’s son from Gundagai  
Said, “Christ, I want my mother.”  
The stranger smiled through dust and tears:  
“I know, my little brother.”

At mess they toasted God and King,  
And markets yet unopened;  
They spoke of honour, race, and trade,  
With rhetoric well-soapened.  
But down below, where corpses slept  
In democratic weather,  
The saints and sinners, Turk and Anzac,  
Were quite at peace together.

“Recruiting’s down,” the major sighed,  
“We need a holy poster:  
A saviour with an Aussie grin,  
A halo near the coaster.  
We’ll put him charging up the heights,  
A bayonet fixed and splendid!”  
The stranger said, “I carried wood.  
I know how these things ended.”

They dressed him in a slouch hat then,  
Pinned badges to his tunic,  
And posed him where the shells fell short  
For papers patriotic.  
“Smile,” they said, “for home and church,  
For empire’s sacred story.”  
He looked toward the hospital ships  
And would not smile for glory.

By evening word had spread around:  
A prophet in the trenches!  
Some asked for luck, some asked for leave,  
Some asked for rum and wenches.  
He gave no medals, cursed no Turks,  
Made no recruiting thunder—  
Just broke his bread with hungry men  
And split their pride asunder.

The chaplain found him near the wire,  
Where moonlight silvered slaughter,  
Washing a dead Ottoman’s face  
With his own rationed water.  
“Careful,” hissed the holy man  
Of empire-sanctioned pity,  
“The newspapers may not approve  
Such indiscreet Christianity.”

At last the brass grew tired of him—  
His silence proved seditious;  
His mercy lacked a proper flag,  
His grief was injudicious.  
“You weaken morale,” the colonel snapped.  
“You blur the cause we fight for.”  
The stranger said, “I often do  
The things you nail me tight for.”

So when they quit that bitter shore,  
With frost and failure biting,  
They left him where the poppies learned  
A red beyond reciting.  
No dispatch named his quiet work,  
No monument stood near him;  
But every mother’s candle knew,  
And every widow’d hear him.

And still, when nations oil the drums  
And polish old salvation,  
When pulpits fit a bayonet  
To Sunday’s consolation,  
He walks among the doomed again,  
Long-haired, unsold, unsteady—  
Not blessing flags or emperors,  
But asking, “Are you ready

To love the man they call your foe,  
To doubt the songs they sold you,  
To see the cross in every grave  
The recruiting bands foretold you?”  
Then guns reply, and preachers cheer,  
And kings applaud the thunder—  
While Christ goes barefoot through the mud,  
With all the boys thereunder.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an anti-war monologue from an ANZAC soldier describing a strange recruit with long hair who becomes terrifyingly effective with a bayonet, using understated Australian diction.
counterfactuals.output:
I remember him turning up late, which was about the first sensible thing he did.

We were already in camp, learning how to stand straight, turn left, turn right, and get shouted at by men with moustaches who seemed to think the Empire would collapse if your bootlaces weren’t tied in the approved fashion. Then this bloke comes wandering in with hair down near his shoulders, like he’d taken a wrong turn on the way to a shearing shed or a travelling show.

No one knew what to make of him. He wasn’t big. Not small either. Just sort of there. Quiet. Had eyes that didn’t settle much. The sergeant took one look at the hair and said something unprintable, and the lad just nodded, as if he’d been told it might rain.

We called him Bluey, naturally, because his hair was dark as a crow. That’s the sort of wit the army produces when it isn’t busy producing widows.

He didn’t drink much. Didn’t sing. Didn’t write many letters, so far as I saw. When the rest of us were yarning about home—Maitland, Ballarat, Dunedin, little places with big skies—he’d sit off a bit and run his thumb along the seam of his trousers. Not nervous, exactly. More like he was listening to something the rest of us couldn’t hear.

At first we reckoned he’d be useless.

Then they gave us bayonets.

You have to understand, they talked about the bayonet like it was a grand old thing. Steel and spirit, they said. Cold courage. The final argument. All that rot. Officers loved phrases like that. They didn’t say what it really was: a knife on the end of a rifle, made so one frightened man could shove it into another frightened man before the second fellow did the same to him.

Most of us trained like men chopping wood in a dream. Lunge, recover. Butt stroke. Parry. Shout while you do it, because apparently murder needed a bit of theatre.

Bluey watched.

Then he had a go.

Well.

The instructor stopped smiling.

There was nothing flashy about it. That was the worst of it, I think. No wild yelling, no mad eyes, none of the stuff they put on posters. Bluey moved like he’d found the one job his body had been waiting for. The rifle sat in his hands as if it had grown there. He’d step, turn, slip aside, and the sandbag would jump and sag and spill its guts. Again. Again. Again.

“Good,” said the instructor, after a while, though he didn’t sound pleased.

The rest of us clapped and jeered because that’s what you do when you’re twenty and scared of silence. Bluey just looked at the bag, breathing through his nose.

After that, they used him for demonstrations.

“Watch this man,” they said.

So we did.

We watched him put steel into sacks, into straw men, into hanging bundles of old uniforms stuffed with rags. We watched officers nod. We watched the sergeants grin as if they’d discovered a new kind of plough. We watched a quiet, odd young bloke become useful to the war.

That’s the part that turns my stomach now. Not that he was strange. Plenty of us were strange, once the guns started. Not that he was good with a bayonet. A man can be good at any damned thing if the world is foolish enough to teach him.

It was the pride.

We were proud of him.

There’s a recruit, we thought. There’s a hard case. There’s one for the Turks or the Germans or whoever they point us at next. We slapped him on the back and told him he’d be right. We made a little legend of him before he’d even left the camp. Long-haired Bluey, quiet as a church, quick as a snake.

And he let us. Not because he liked it. I don’t think he liked anything much by then. But because saying no to the army is like telling the tide to pull its head in.

Later, at the front, there wasn’t much legend left in anyone.

Mud takes it out of you. So does lack of sleep. So does seeing a man you played cards with sitting in a trench with his hand pressed to his neck, looking surprised, as if death had broken some social rule. The big words all shrank over there. Honour. Glory. Sacrifice. They got smaller and smaller until they were just noises made by people a long way from the stink.

Bluey’s hair got cropped in the end. Lice did what the sergeant couldn’t. He looked younger without it, which was no help.

I saw him in a charge once.

I won’t dress it up.

There was smoke and wire and men falling in untidy ways. Someone was screaming for his mother in an accent I couldn’t place. The ground shook like it wanted us off its back. We’d been told to take a trench, as if a trench was a thing that could be taken and not a ditch full of poor bastards with rifles, waiting to make you pay for every yard.

Bluey went ahead.

Not running wild. Just moving. Low and quick. He reached the lip before most of us. A shape rose in front of him and Bluey’s rifle went forward and back, neat as a man opening a gate. Another came at him from the side. Bluey turned. Same again.

It was terrible because it was efficient.

That’s the word. Efficient. Like loading crates. Like cutting cane. Like some honest labour had been twisted until it became this.

When we got into the trench, I saw his face. No triumph there. No bloodlust. He looked weary, and faintly puzzled, as if he’d been asked to do sums in a language he didn’t know. There was blood on his sleeve. Some of it his. Most not.

One of our corporals said, “Good work, Blue.”

Bluey nodded.

Good work.

That’s what we called it.

I’ve thought about that for years. Good work. As if the world hadn’t come apart in our hands. As if the dead men at our feet hadn’t also had names, and mothers, and some little habit at breakfast that annoyed their sisters. As if Bluey had done something fine instead of something we’d trained him into, praised him for, and then left him to carry.

He didn’t last the year. Not because of a bayonet. Shell got him. Shells didn’t care what you were good at. They made no study of character. Brave, coward, saint, mongrel, long hair, short back and sides—it was all the same to them. A bit of iron arrived from nowhere and settled the matter.

We found what we could.

Someone said he’d been a good soldier.

I suppose he was.

That’s the bloody shame of it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a literary pastiche combining a historical church endorsement of World War I with a modern free-verse narrative of Jesus fighting alongside Australian soldiers at Gallipoli.
counterfactuals.output:
**A Pastiche: “At Anzac Cove, Under the Benediction”**

Brethren,  
in this grave and searching hour,  
when Empire’s trumpet sounds across the seas  
and sons of the parish stand beneath the flag,  
let none among us shrink from duty.  

For the sword is not borne in vain  
when righteousness is imperilled,  
nor is sacrifice strange  
to those who kneel beneath the Cross.  

We commend, therefore,  
our young men to the keeping of Almighty God:  
that He may strengthen their arms,  
purify their intentions,  
comfort their mothers,  
and grant victory to the cause of justice and peace.  

Let the bells be rung,  
let the hymns be lifted,  
let every loyal heart remember  
that to serve King and Country  
is, in this solemn hour,  
to serve the purposes of Providence.

Amen.

---

But down at Gallipoli  
the morning did not sound like an anthem.

It came in shrapnel,  
in flies,  
in salt stiffening the uniforms  
of boys who had learned the word *duty*  
from pulpits, posters, fathers,  
and the hard bright mouths of schoolmasters.

The boats scraped stone.  
The cliffs rose like a question  
no bishop had answered.

And Jesus was there—

not in a stained-glass window,  
not holding a banner,  
not blessing the guns from a clean distance,

but barefoot in the landing water,  
his robe dark with the Aegean,  
his hands already full of blood  
that was not metaphor.

He did not look like victory.

He looked like a stretcher-bearer  
who had not slept for three days.  
He looked like a mate from Ballarat,  
a shearer from Bourke,  
a clerk from Melbourne  
with terror in his teeth  
and mercy in his eyes.

“Keep low,” he said,  
though the bullets did not keep low.

He took the arm of a boy  
calling for his mother  
and pressed a canteen to his lips.  
He knelt beside a Turk  
and an Australian  
so close in death  
their boots touched,  
and he closed both their eyes  
with the same two fingers.

Above them,  
chaplains prayed for courage.  
Generals unfolded maps.  
The sea kept bringing in more sons.

Jesus climbed the ridge  
without a rifle.

This made no sense  
to anyone.

A corporal shouted,  
“Get down, you bloody fool,”  
and Jesus smiled  
as if he had heard  
something like that before  
in another garden,  
on another night  
when men with weapons came.

He lifted no sword.  
Still, he fought.

He fought the thirst.  
He fought the panic.  
He fought the lie  
that a man becomes holy  
by killing another frightened man  
because someone far away  
has dressed the order in Scripture.

He fought by carrying.  
He fought by binding.  
He fought by standing  
between the living and despair.

And when the barrage opened  
and the hill shook loose its stones,  
he was seen—  
or later they said he was seen—  
dragging Private Thomas Keane  
of the 8th Battalion  
back through scrub and dust,

one hand beneath the boy’s shoulders,  
one hand pressed over the wound  
as if holding the world together.

The boy whispered,  
“Are we winning?”

Jesus looked toward the beach,  
where the gulls circled  
over the wreckage of prayers.

“No,” he said.  
“Not yet.”

Then softer:

“But you are not alone.”

---

O God of Battles,  
the newspapers wrote,  
receive our noble dead.

O Prince of Peace,  
the mothers wrote,  
send my son home.

O Christ,  
the soldiers wrote nowhere,  
because the pencils snapped,  
because the paper got wet,  
because some words cannot survive  
the mouth that must speak them.

Yet in the trench,  
under biscuit tins and sandbags,  
someone had scratched into the clay:

**Blessed are the poor bloody infantry.**

And beneath it,  
in another hand:

**Blessed are the merciful.**

By August,  
even the prayers were gaunt.

The endorsement still rang  
in parish halls half a world away—  
noble cause,  
Christian duty,  
sacred sacrifice,  
the glory of service.

But at Anzac Cove  
glory had the smell of iodine  
and unburied heat.

Jesus sat with the wounded  
when the flies came.

He tore strips from his own garment.  
He washed feet gone black with mud.  
He listened to confessions  
that were mostly silence.

A boy said,  
“I don’t want to hate them.”

Jesus answered,  
“Then don’t.”

A boy said,  
“I’m afraid.”

Jesus answered,  
“So was I.”

A boy said,  
“Will God forgive us?”

And Jesus looked across no-man’s-land  
to where another chaplain  
was asking the same question  
in Turkish,

and he said,

“God has been here  
longer than the guns.”

---

Therefore, beloved brethren,  
let us honour the fallen.

But let us not polish death  
until it shines like virtue.

Let us not make Christ  
a recruiting sergeant  
with a halo for a badge.

If he came to Gallipoli,  
he came as he always comes:

among the poor,  
the pierced,  
the condemned,  
the terrified,  
the tender-hearted  
who still pass water to the enemy  
because thirst is older than nations.

He came not to bless the bayonet  
but to receive the body.

Not to crown the Empire  
but to cradle the boy.

Not to explain the war  
but to enter it,  
and by entering,  
to judge it.

And the hills heard him.

The sea heard him.

The dead, who were beyond enlistment,  
heard him.

At evening,  
when the firing thinned  
and the stretcher-bearers moved  
like shadows through the scrub,  
Jesus stood at the waterline  
looking homeward with the Australians,

toward mothers,  
toward farms,  
toward streets where church bells waited  
to call the faithful again  
to courage,  
to mourning,  
to memory.

He raised his hand.

Not in salute.

In blessing.

And the blessing fell  
not on the war,  
but on every broken thing  
the war had made.
